utterances.text: [music]
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: In 1960, when a young English woman named Jane Goodall set out to study chimpanzees in the
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: forests of Tanzania, she broke all the rules about the study of animals in the wild. And as a result,
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: she opened a whole new window into the lives of wild animals and shattered our accepted notions
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: of what it meant to be human. The work made her a world celebrity. Alarmed at what human beings
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: were doing to the world we share with other life, Goodall established the Jane Goodall Institute in
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: 1977 with the objective of protecting chimpanzees and their habitats and, by extension, other forms
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: of life. The Institute now has 19 offices around the world. In 1991, the Institute created a global
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: youth program called Roots and Shoots, which now consists of more than 10,000 groups in over 100
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: countries. One of Goodall's most brilliant ideas is that the conservation of nature and the
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: sustainable development of human communities are inextricably linked together, a concept that
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: underlies much of her continuing work at the chimpanzee site in Africa. Roots and Shoots began
utterances.speaker: speaker-1

utterances.text: in 1991 in Tanzania with a group of 12 high school students. And they came to learn more
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: about animals because they weren't learning at school and they weren't learning anything about
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: the environment at school. So we talked about all these things and they became increasingly shocked
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: and eventually decided, well, they would like to do something about some of these things
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: themselves since governments weren't and the schools weren't. And so we started a sort of
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: club and they went back and got some friends involved. And that's how it began very simply
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: because the chimpanzee was always, in a way, linking humans with the rest of the animal kingdom.
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: Right from the beginning, it was, well, choose projects that will help people, help animals,
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: help the environment. We all share three different kinds of project. And it didn't grow very fast,
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: but then suddenly it began to take off like the mid-90s. And it's now in 126 countries with about
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: 16,000 active groups with membership from preschool through college, through university,
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: more and more adults forming groups. Basically, every single one of us matters. Every single
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: one of us makes a difference every single day. And if we would think about the consequences of
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: the little choices we make, what we eat, what we buy, what we wear, you know, people then begin to
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: make small changes. And it's when thousands, then millions start making the small changes that we
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: get the kind of change we need. But the name is symbolic. And if you imagine a big tree,
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: and then when it starts to grow, little roots from a seed and a little shoot,
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: and you can pick it up and it seems so weak and so frail. But there is a magic, a life force,
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: a power in that little seed so strong that those little roots to reach the water can work through
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: rocks and eventually push them aside. And that little shoot to reach the sunlight can work
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: through cracks in a brick wall and eventually knock it down. So we see the rocks and the walls
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: as all the problems we have inflicted on the planet, environmental and social. Then it's hope.
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: Hundreds and thousands of young people around the world can break through and make this a better
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: place for all living things. Because without hope, there is no hope. If our youth loses hope,
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: we may as well give up. And you've heard a lot of youth that have lost hope. I was meeting so
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: many young people who'd lost hope. And that was why it seemed important to develop this
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: Roots and Toots program. Now what may I say to you, Dr. Jane, do you have hope? And you
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: reply yes. And then they say why? What do you say then? I tell people who ask me if I have hope,
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: and it's a question I get asked all the time, that I've got four very simple, naive reasons.
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: Firstly, the human brain. We know it's capable of doing very unpleasant things like weapons
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: of mass destruction. But it's also creating incredible technology. And I really believe
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: that people are finally understanding the harm we've inflicted on the planet. And a feeling
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: of sense of urgency with climate change, global warming, and so forth. And when our backs are to
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: the wall, the human beings, the brain's always worked over time. And I think this is happening.
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: And there are more technologies that will enable us to leave a less disastrous environmental
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: footprint, both businesses and individuals. So that's one reason for hope. Second reason
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: is the resilience of nature. We can just about completely destroy a river or a forest or a
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: wetland or whatever it is, but give it time, perhaps give it help, perhaps put a lot of money
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: into it, whatever, but it can come back. Maybe not exactly as it was, but it can support life
utterances.speaker: speaker-2

utterances.text: and become beautiful again. For The Green Interview, I'm Silver Donald Cameron. See you next time.
utterances.speaker: speaker-2
